content.text: Chapter Fifteen
Oaths Severed
The second Scryer testimony reached Silvermoon before the first had finished producing rumors.

Halduron’s rangers brought the witnesses through the eastern relay under concealment: a Sunfury quartermaster with burns up both hands, and a spellwright who had served in Tempest Keep’s southern wing until Kael’thas’s soldiers turned its guns upon their former allies. Their statements differed in dates, unit strengths, and the names of officers who had survived. They agreed on the Legion envoys. They agreed on fel armaments entering Netherstorm under the prince’s seals. Most damningly, they agreed that no order had been issued to restore contact with Quel’Thalas.

By dusk, Rommath had authenticated six more ciphers. By midnight, Astalor had proved that one of the unfamiliar command marks on Voren’thal’s dispatches was layered over a royal transit seal. Before dawn, Lor’themar summoned the council.

Falanaras stood inside the chamber doors with Theron at his right hand. Blood Knight plate was ceremonial only to those who had never waited through a council deciding whether soldiers would become enemies. The black armor held heat beneath the crimson tabard. M’uru’s presence rested within Falanaras as a muted ache, distant beneath layers of stone and force-work. Each time he drew breath, the personal bond answered with enough warmth to remind him what Kael’thas had sent home—and what Silvermoon had chosen to do with the gift.

The council table had disappeared beneath testimony, copied seals, troop ledgers, and a map of Outland crowded with black stones. Lor’themar occupied the head without a throne behind him. Halduron stood over the Hellfire approaches. Rommath and Astalor had taken the Netherstorm side, where red ink marked seized installations and vanished supply posts. Liadrin remained seated with both hands bare upon the table. The gold beneath her green eyes had sharpened during the sleepless days since Voren’thal’s letter.
Lor’themar waited until the doors were sealed. “State only what can be defended.”

Rommath’s hand moved over the nearest documents. “Kael’thas broke Illidan’s command, seized strategic holdings in Netherstorm, and redirected Sunfury stores to forces answering solely to him. Demonic representatives entered Tempest Keep beneath protection. Fel weapons arrived through channels concealed from his established command structure. These matters are independently attested and supported by authenticated records.”
“His agreement with the Legion?” Halduron asked.
“Still hidden,” Rommath said. “We know there is intercourse. We do not know its terms. Any proclamation naming a sworn allegiance would outrun the evidence.”

Halduron tapped the empty road between the Dark Portal and the western reaches. “He permitted this kingdom to remain blind for eleven months. After the road reopened, he sent no warning that demons held it. Whatever terms he made, our patrols cannot assume his troops are friendly.”

“Some may still be,” Liadrin said. “Sanguinar is not the whole of them.” Her voice tightened around the name. “There are soldiers in Outland who took their oaths before any demon entered the prince’s halls. There are three Blood Knights beside Sanguinar whose judgment I have no cause to condemn.”
“Can you close their binding?” Lor’themar asked.
Astalor answered. “No. The bindings were designed to survive distance, interruption, and hostile transit. A virtue at the time.”
Liadrin looked at him. “Do you regret that?”

“Regret does not alter the mechanism.” Astalor’s gaze stayed upon the layered seal he had exposed. “If they draw, M’uru supplies them and suffers. If they waste the current, continue beyond purpose, or use it for cruelty, distance gives us no means to stop them. Our ignorance of their conduct does not interrupt any of those facts.”

The chamber fell quiet enough for Falanaras to hear the low thrum of the wards. He remembered Sanguinar smiling after Daric’s shoulder broke beneath red-gold Light. The injury had been deliberate, the excess a pleasure disguised as instruction. Kael’thas had not witnessed it. He had still chosen the man who committed it.

“There is another question,” one of the senior magistrates said. “If ruthless acquisition is proof of corruption, we should consider where that judgment leads.” His eyes went briefly toward Liadrin, then lower, toward the hidden vault beneath the city.

No one mistook the reference. The Light shifted under Falanaras’s ribs. He felt a thin echo of M’uru’s fracture and resisted the instinct to close himself against it. Forgetting the pain would make the bond easier. Liadrin had never promised ease.
Astalor turned from the seal. “The distinction is uncomplicated.”
“I doubt that,” Liadrin said.

“Kael’thas’s methods did not become intolerable because they were cruel. Cruelty may be efficient, wasteful, necessary, or indulgent according to its result.” Astalor spoke with the same precision he used when measuring a current through living flesh. “His methods became treasonous when the survival of Quel’Thalas ceased to govern them. He continues to invoke the kingdom while withholding information, stores, command, and protection from it. The stated purpose remains. The actual beneficiary has changed.”
The senior magistrate’s mouth tightened. “A convenient line for those of us standing over a captive naaru.”

“Convenience has no bearing on accuracy.” Astalor did not look away. “M’uru’s captivity feeds our wards, heals our wounded, quiets the hunger of every knight bound below, and may yet relieve more of the city if the conduits can be corrected. The suffering is real. So is the service to Quel’Thalas. If those facts change, our justification changes with them.”
Liadrin’s fingers curled once against the table. “And who decides when service becomes appetite?”
“Those willing to keep measuring after they have obtained the answer they wanted.”

Falanaras had heard colder things from Astalor. Few had troubled him more. The argument left Silvermoon’s compromises intact and set a boundary around them, yet the boundary depended upon the same hands already taking the power. Rynel had spent what the escape required, then turned the strength away from his hunger and toward the soldiers depending on him. Sanguinar had continued after the agreed purpose ended because suffering pleased him. Between those choices lay an entire kingdom’s claim to discipline and honor.

Lor’themar gathered the testimony into a single stack. “We are not judging whether Kael’thas has sinned more elegantly than we have. We are deciding whose commands can be allowed to spend blood elf lives.”
He looked first to Halduron. “Can our forces in Outland obey the prince without endangering Quel’Thalas?”
“No,” Halduron said. “Any unit claiming his authority must be treated as potentially hostile until it submits to Silvermoon’s command and disarms for examination.”
“Can the magisters continue sharing transit ciphers, stores, or strategic intelligence with his command?”

“No,” Rommath said. The word cost him nothing visible. He had carried Kael’thas’s methods home, defended them, and built Silvermoon’s recovery around what the prince’s followers had learned in exile. “All royal ciphers tied to Outland will be revoked. The relay architecture will be altered before sunset. Any message bearing the prince’s seal will be contained and examined rather than obeyed.”
Lor’themar turned to Liadrin. “If Sanguinar or another Blood Knight acts under Kael’thas’s command against this kingdom?”
The gold in her eyes brightened. “Then the oath has already been broken. My knights will answer force with force.”

At last Lor’themar looked to the table as a whole. “Kael’thas Sunstrider remains the son of our king and the prince to whom this people gave its hope. He no longer commands Quel’Thalas. His faction in Outland will be regarded as unfriendly until its members renounce concealed allegiances and submit to lawful examination. No soldier, magister, ranger, or civil officer in this kingdom will obey his seal.”

The words did not sound like the fall of a dynasty. They sounded like orders read before a march. Falanaras found that harder to bear. Kael’thas had survived the Scourge, exile, Garithos, and Outland long enough to become the future tense of every blood elf promise. Now Lor’themar removed that future with a sequence of practical restrictions.
No one voted. Each answer had already been given.
The phoenix above the Court of the Sun came down at noon.

Officials had removed smaller royal banners from military halls and relay offices before the proclamation was posted. Those disappearances could be overlooked as caution. The great standard could not. It hung from the highest arch in restored Silvermoon, crimson silk worked with a gold phoenix broad enough to catch fire at sunset. Kael’thas had not raised it with his own hands. Most citizens had never seen him stand beneath it. They had still looked up and believed the kingdom’s road led back to him.

Falanaras commanded the Blood Knight cordon around the square. Theron held the western stair with six shield-bearers. City guards lined the proclamation boards, and Rommath’s magisters stood at intervals beneath the colonnades, their hands empty and their sleeves marked with active restraint sigils. The preparation told the crowd how the government expected grief to behave.

Two workers climbed the arch. When the first fastening released, the phoenix leaned over the Court as though straining to see the faces below. A sound moved through the gathered citizens—too low for a shout, too rough for prayer.
“Leave it,” someone called.

The second fastening came free. Wind entered the silk and lifted one golden wing. Citizens pressed against the cordon. Falanaras smelled perfume, hot metal, mana crystals opened too early in anxious hands. The hunger threaded through the square beneath the anger: shallow breathing, fixed attention, the fine tremor of people who had waited through the morning rather than leave their place near an active ward.

Lor’themar stepped onto the annex balcony as the workers began lowering the banner. He wore no ceremonial mantle. Halduron stood behind him in ranger leathers, Rommath in dark magisterial robes, and Liadrin in black plate. Their presence offered the city every form of authority it possessed except the one being taken down.

Lor’themar read the proclamation without ceremony. He named the verified break with Illidan, the seizure of Tempest Keep, demonic contact, diverted resources, and the failure to communicate with the kingdom. He did not accuse Kael’thas of serving the Legion. He did not call him mad, fallen, or traitor. The restraint denied the crowd an easy lie to attack.

“Until the prince submits his conduct and alliances to examination,” Lor’themar concluded, “his seals hold no authority within Quel’Thalas. Forces acting in his name beyond our borders are to be regarded as unfriendly. The defense and governance of this kingdom remain under the Regent Lord and the lawful offices of Silvermoon.”

A woman near the front began to weep without covering her face. Behind her, a veteran raised a clenched fist and shouted that Lor’themar had usurped the crown. Another voice demanded the evidence be shown in the square. A third called Voren’thal a draenei servant. The accusations multiplied faster than the guards could identify their sources.
The banner reached the lower ledge. A young man broke from the crowd and ran for it.

Falanaras intercepted him before the first stair. He caught the man across the chest and turned the charge aside. They struck the paving hard enough to jar his armor. The man had no weapon. He clawed at Falanaras’s gauntlet and stared past him toward the descending phoenix.
“My sister followed him,” he gasped. “You cannot make her a traitor because she believed what all of you told us.”
Falanaras held him while two city guards approached. The square had blurred around the rawness in his face. “Your sister has not been judged.”
“You said his forces are enemies.”
“Unfriendly until they submit. Those were the words.”
“Words.” The man laughed once, breathless and broken. “You put armor around words so the rest of us have to call them law.”

The guards took his arms. Falanaras ordered them to hold him for questioning and record that he had carried no weapon. It was the narrowest mercy available within the duty. The man disappeared behind the cordon still watching the phoenix fold into the workers’ hands.
By the time Lor’themar withdrew from the balcony, the crowd had begun chanting Kael’thas’s name.
For three days, Silvermoon argued with the proclamation.

Copies appeared with lines crossed out and kinder words written above them. Demonic contact became coerced negotiation. Diverted stores became preparation for a greater return. Eleven months of silence became proof that Kael’thas had been imprisoned by enemies who now forged his seals. Someone circulated a letter claiming the prince had ordered Silvermoon evacuated to Outland and Lor’themar had suppressed it to preserve his regency. The letter used a royal cipher revoked six years earlier. Hundreds believed it before noon.

Outland recovered its old place in the city’s imagination. People described terraces in Netherstorm where no one hungered, estates waiting beneath violet skies, armies gathering to reclaim the Sunwell. Hellfire’s Legion emplacements disappeared from these accounts. So did the abandoned Sunfury station and the empty road. Outland had been promised too long to surrender to geography.

Falanaras moved between duties with Theron beside him: the annex at dawn, the western mana queue by midday, Murder Row after dark. Liadrin assigned them where black armor might end a dispute before drawn weapons did. Sometimes it worked. More often the sight of Blood Knights proved only that the government had brought M’uru’s power to defend its judgment.

On the fourth morning, they found a royal phoenix painted across the doors of a ration hall. The guards had covered it with canvas, but citizens lifted the edge as they passed and touched two fingers to the red paint. A bowl of mana shards sat beneath it as an offering. Most were poor pieces, cloudy from repeated use. One still held enough charge to ease a family through the night.
“That may be the saddest shrine I have ever guarded,” Theron said.
Falanaras watched an attendant carry the bowl inside for inspection. “You have guarded a shrine with a chained naaru beneath it.”
“That one has better funding.” Theron’s humor faded. “Do you think they are all wrong?”
“About the evidence?”
“About needing him to remain what we said he was.”

Falanaras looked toward the upper towers. Empty clasps showed where royal standards had hung. “No. We built too much of ourselves around his return. Belief does not become stupidity because the person trusted proved false.”
“You should tell them that.”
“They would hear the armor first.”
Theron rested one hand on the rim of his shield. “Then I will stand farther away and look decorative.”

The ration hall doors opened before Falanaras could answer. A runner emerged at speed with orders bearing Rommath’s seal. A gathering had formed outside the old pilgrims’ hospice near the southern market. Witnesses reported weapons, plans to seize a relay chamber, and promises of passage through the Dark Portal.
Theron read over Falanaras’s shoulder. “I withdraw my offer.”

The hospice had once housed families waiting to follow Kael’thas into Outland. Its courtyard was built around a dry fountain, with narrow galleries rising on three sides and a single gate opening onto the market. More than a hundred citizens had packed inside by the time the Blood Knights arrived. Phoenix cloth hung from the upper railings. At the fountain, a former Sunfury officer stood upon the basin and read from the forged evacuation order.

Rommath’s magisters had reached the side streets first. They sealed both ends of the market with translucent walls and laid restraint glyphs beneath the paving. City guards waited behind Falanaras’s line. Their captain reported six visible swords, perhaps twice as many knives, and three spellcasters in the galleries. No relay chamber had yet been attacked.

“Then we disperse them before they try,” said Magister Varethis, the officer commanding Rommath’s detail. He was young enough that Falanaras remembered him carrying messages during the reconstruction. Power had since smoothed his voice and put silver rank marks on his collar. “Captain Dawnspear, place your knights across the gate. No one leaves until examined.”

Falanaras studied the courtyard. Children stood among the adults. An elderly woman had brought a camp stool. Two men carrying swords wore them with the awkward care of heirlooms rather than practiced weapons. “Give them a path to leave peacefully.”
“They have gathered in defiance of an emergency order.”
“Half of them will have come to listen. Let the unarmed depart one at a time under guard. Arrest those who remain or resist.”
Varethis considered him for a breath. “One warning.”

Falanaras entered the gate with Theron and eight Blood Knights. Conversation faltered as black plate filled the opening. The former officer at the fountain lowered the forged order. He wore an old campaign sash over civilian clothes, its red faded almost brown.

“This assembly is unlawful,” Falanaras said. “Lay down weapons. Those who submit to search may leave in single file. Anyone attempting the relay stations, raising magic, or resisting the guard will be detained.”
“Detained for loyalty?” the officer asked.
“For threatening a secured relay and carrying weapons into a prohibited gathering.”
“The relay belongs to the prince.”
“It belongs to the kingdom that built and defends it.”
The officer raised the forged page. “He called us to Outland. You went. You returned with power and shut the road behind you.”

Anger stirred through the courtyard. Falanaras felt his knights respond: shields shifting, hands settling on hilts, bonds of power opening by disciplined degrees. M’uru’s pain brushed the edge of his awareness as red-gold light gathered beneath black gauntlets. Effective. Immediate. Another captive answer to fear.

“I went because Kael’thas summoned a soldier to replace a dead man,” he said. “I returned because he sent M’uru to Silvermoon. I fought under his command. I heard the evidence against him from those who served closer than I did. The page in your hand is false.”
“According to Rommath.”
“According to a cipher I carried on my own orders before I crossed the sea. That sequence was retired before the Dark Portal opened for us.”

The certainty disturbed the crowd more than accusation had. Several people looked toward the gate. The elderly woman folded her stool. A father lifted his child onto one hip and began edging through the bodies.
Then one of the gallery spellcasters cast.

The bolt struck Theron’s shield and broke into violet fire. He had moved before Falanaras saw the lifted hand. Red-gold radiance curved across the gate, shielding the nearest civilians as the other Blood Knights locked into line. Falanaras reached into the spell as it collapsed against the barrier and took a bounded measure of its loose arcane power. The caster in the gallery lifted both hands for a second attack. Falanaras released the stolen charge in a tight blue-white rush. It struck at the opening of the invocation and emptied the words from the man’s mouth. The next spell failed before it formed.
Magister Varethis activated the courtyard.

Silver restraint lines flashed beneath every foot. The paving gripped ankles, knees, wrists. Citizens crashed against one another as the spell forced them downward. A woman struck the basin and split her lip. One Blood Knight caught her before the restraint could wrench her shoulder, pressed two fingers to the cut, and closed it with a brief pulse while the silver bands still held her on her knees. The former officer remained standing for half a heartbeat longer than the rest, then a band of arcane force closed around his throat and dragged him down.

The spellcaster in the gallery tried to speak again. Varethis closed his hand. The man’s jaw snapped shut. Silence wards descended across the courtyard, swallowing cries, orders, even the scrape of armor. A hundred citizens knelt beneath a net they could neither see nor resist.
Falanaras turned on Varethis. His voice vanished inside the ward. The magister read the demand in his face and made a small adjustment. Sound returned around the Blood Knight line alone.
“Release the children and the unarmed,” Falanaras said.
“A spell was cast at your second.”
“By one man. Hold the galleries and those carrying weapons. The others were offered passage.”
Varethis glanced toward the former officer. Arcane pressure had drawn blood beneath his chin. “They heard sedition and remained.”
“Listening is not an attack.”
“Today it became cover for one.” Varethis’s expression remained calm.

It was an argument Falanaras understood. That did not make the woman bleeding against the fountain less real. He could break the restraint web. His spellbreaker senses already found its anchors in the courtyard walls. Doing so would free the armed with the frightened and turn disagreement between officers into open defiance before the crowd.

Theron stood beside him, shield still raised. “If the state waits for every grievance to become an attack, we will fight the city street by street,” he said quietly. “This attack is contained. No need to punish the ones it missed.”

Varethis studied both of them, then lifted two fingers. The restraints loosened around the children first, then around thirty adults nearest the gate. Guards searched and released them in groups of five. The rest remained kneeling while magisters moved among them, touching light to temples and asking names, affiliations, intended routes, known organizers. The answers came through clenched teeth. Some came after the compulsion sigils brightened.

Falanaras watched the former officer resist until his body shook. At last the man named two meeting houses and a clerk inside the western relay office. Varethis recorded each answer. When it was done, the officer sagged against the fountain, conscious but unable to lift his head.
No one called the process torture. Silvermoon had learned to keep its ugliest truths behind accurate administrative language.
The emergency orders were posted that evening.

Assemblies of more than twelve required approval. The relay chambers, city gates, armories, mana distribution halls, and principal ward stations passed under military protection. Travel permits were suspended. A curfew closed the lower markets after second bell. Advocacy of unauthorized passage to Outland was designated incitement to breach the kingdom’s defenses. The phrase martial law appeared nowhere, though soldiers now stood at every place the orders named.

Falanaras read the notice outside the Blood Knight barracks while Theron cleaned a scorch mark from his shield. Around them, patrols prepared to enter streets that had greeted the order as heroes only months before.
“You were right,” Falanaras said.
Theron examined the shield. “This is a rare opening. Be specific.”

“You were right. We would fight street by street if the state waited for every grievance to become an attack.” Falanaras looked toward the Court, where the empty banner clasps caught the last light. “The attack was contained. That is what makes it dangerous.”
Theron set the cloth aside. “We have spent years learning that necessary things can still be dangerous.”
“We say that when we want to keep doing them.”

“Yes.” Theron met his eyes. “We also say it when stopping would leave someone else to pay.” He nodded toward the patrol assembling by the gate. “The question is whether we remember whose pain is being entered into the account.”
M’uru’s distant anguish lived beneath the warmth in Falanaras’s chest. The former officer’s forced answers had no such lasting bond. That made them easier for the city to forget.
A messenger arrived before first bell with a summons to the council chamber. This time Theron was included.

The evidence against Kael’thas had been cleared from the table. In its place lay maps of the Eastern Kingdoms: Quel’Thalas isolated at the northern edge, the Ghostlands below it, hostile territories and ruined roads stretching south. Halduron’s casualty ledgers sat open beside reports from the runestone boundary. Rommath had arranged reserve estimates in descending columns. None reached far into the year.

“Kael’thas gave this kingdom an answer to hunger and a road beyond its enemies,” Lor’themar said. “We have severed the road. M’uru remains, but the distribution program is still limited, and the forces beyond the Portal can no longer be counted as ours. We must replace what we have lost before our enemies discover the absence.”

Halduron named the borders first. The runestone line had held, though Scourge pressure continued along the Dead Scar. Amani warbands were testing Farstrider patrols more boldly. The Ghostlands remained unheld, its roads usable only by armed movements. Silvermoon could defend southern Eversong against a single incursion. Two simultaneous breaches would force choices measured in villages.

Rommath named what assistance would not come. The Alliance had neither forgotten Garithos nor forgiven the sin’dorei’s methods, and its scattered contacts had shown more interest in observation than defense. The Kirin Tor would debate jurisdiction until the Dead Scar reached their doors. The Argent Dawn might cooperate against the Scourge, but neutrality prevented the political and military commitment Quel’Thalas needed. Shattrath lay beyond a demon-held Portal and could offer witnesses sooner than armies.
“Then we have no allies,” Liadrin said.
“We have no allies we would have chosen,” Lor’themar replied.

Halduron placed a black marker south of the runestone boundary. “Forsaken scouts continue operating in the Ghostlands. Serenya Duskrunner’s unit has honored the warning signals established after the Eversong incursion. They have shared Scourge movements twice and accepted our demand to withdraw south after contact.”
Liadrin rose so abruptly her chair struck the wall. Light flashed beneath her skin. “Field signals are not an alliance. They are corpses wearing the memories of our rangers.”

“They are soldiers who helped keep an undead host from cutting farther into Eversong,” Halduron said. His voice held the quiet firmness of someone accustomed to speaking across old wounds. “Their arrows killed the necromancer controlling it. Their scouts pulled our wounded clear.”

Falanaras remembered Serenya’s gray face beneath a dark hood, Lethira’s arrow following her mark, Forsaken hands hauling injured Farstriders out of the abomination’s reach. Liadrin remembered different dead: friends raised against their own walls, the Scourge taking holy ground beneath Arthas’s command. Both memories were true. Only one had occurred recently enough to serve as policy.
Rommath moved another marker into the Ghostlands. “The Forsaken answer to Sylvanas Windrunner. Through her, they possess ties to the Horde.”

The name carried the old horror into the chamber. The Horde had come north once before, orcs marching beside Amani warbands that burned through the border forests during the Second War. Falanaras knew that invasion through veterans’ accounts, memorial rolls, and stretches of woodland that had taken decades to mend. Now the same word arrived through Sylvanas Windrunner. He saw Lethira during Silvermoon’s fall, staring after the ranger-general who had been murdered and raised. Sylvanas had once embodied Quel’Thalas’s defense. Whatever ruled the Forsaken had emerged from that desecration with her skill, her hatred, and her claim upon the land still intact.
“You propose asking the Banshee Queen to save Silvermoon,” Liadrin said.
Lor’themar looked down at the map of a kingdom bordered by enemies and memory. “I propose asking what her help costs.”

He ordered Halduron to prepare a complete account of every field contact with the Forsaken. Lethira would be questioned about Serenya and the reliability of her signals. Rommath would calculate what military and magical aid Silvermoon could offer in return. No envoy would depart yet. The city had only begun mourning one promised savior; Lor’themar would not offer it another before he knew the terms.

When the council ended, Falanaras and Theron crossed the Court beneath bare arches. Patrol lamps burned along every street. A pair of magisters questioned a bookseller beside a shuttered stall while guards searched the rooms above it. Farther on, workers scraped a painted phoenix from white stone. Red pigment clung in the chisel marks.
“What do we call this oath?” Theron asked. “The one after the prince.”

Falanaras had sworn to the Blood Knights beneath stolen radiance. Before that, he had sworn to serve a kingdom whose king was dead and whose prince had been far away. Those words had seemed to point in the same direction. Now the kingdom, the order, and the prince stood on separate roads.
“The same one,” he said. “We serve Quel’Thalas.”
Theron watched the magisters lead the bookseller away. “That answer is doing a great deal of work.”
“It always has.”

They continued toward the barracks. Behind them, the last royal phoenix in the Court disappeared beneath the workers’ tools. Ahead, beyond the restored walls and the runestone line, the Ghostlands waited with its Scourge, its ruins, and the undead rangers who had once defended Silvermoon in life.
Quel’Thalas had severed itself from the prince who promised its future. By morning, it would begin counting the monsters close enough to help preserve one.
